explanations.explanation: This feature fires on tokens composed of non-ASCII/Latin‐alphabet characters—e.g. Cyrillic, Japanese/Chinese script, Devanagari, special Unicode punctuation or emojis—marking points where the text switches into or includes foreign‐language or otherwise non-Latin Unicode sequences.

This neuron fires on the little “header” or metadata markers you see in blog/news pages and similar web templates—stand-alone capitalized labels and acronyms (e.g. RSS, Posted, Filed, slides, Adobe, etc.) that frame the structure of entries, feeds and section headings.

This neuron flags the appearance of non-ASCII or “foreign” character tokens – e.g. Hangul syllables, Arabic and Persian letters, Chinese ideographs, Tamil glyphs, accented Latin (œ) and other special‐Unicode symbols – essentially marking the entry of any non-basic-ASCII script or diacritic in the text.

This neuron fires on semantically “heavy” subword tokens—especially derivational affixes (e.g. –inc, –acy, –ability, –ive, –ing) as well as standalone intensifiers and content words (even, well, increasing, creative, Taiwan)—i.e. it marks the onset of lexically salient or emphatic material.

This neuron detects the grammatical “head” of a new clause or headline—the main predicate or topic‐introducing content word. It reliably lights up on past‐tense auxiliaries (did, had), primary verbs (came, told, organized), and sentence-initial content tokens (dateline cities, headline nouns), marking where a new event or topic begins.
This neuron fires on the “headline” bits of text – subword pieces that kick off title-cased words (proper names, event/album/holiday titles, category or label headings, etc.).

This feature fires on parenthesized “metadata” snippets—e.g. model or part numbers, version‐labels, scientific names, acronyms or other inline identifiers—whenever a phrase in parentheses carries that kind of technical or categorical annotation.
This feature detects temporal‐sequencing adverbs (e.g. “earlier,” “later,” “before,” “after”) that explicitly mark an event’s position relative to the current narrative time.

This feature lights up on the single most salient “headline” word in a chunk of text—essentially tagging the key topic or call-to-action (e.g. “Birthday,” “Insurance,” “Summer,” “Answer,” etc.) that serves as the section’s title or thematic pivot.

This feature fires on sentence-initial discourse connectives and adverbial phrases (However, At last, Due to, Accordingly, Finally, Throughout, etc.) that signal transitions, temporal ordering, causality or emphasis in the text.
